paras: The Bald Knobber plot to lynch Almus Harrington was a plan by the Bald Knobbers of Christian County, Missouri, to hang Col. Almus Harrington, an Ozark attorney, in September 1886. A force of 142 men led by the Knobber chief Dave Walker set out toward Ozark to carry out the resolution but abandoned the attack, and Harrington was unharmed. The plot became public in April 1888, when Harrington, then associate counsel for the State in the Bald Knobber cases, described it to a Globe-Democrat correspondent.

By his own account, Harrington had fought the Bald Knobber order "from its birth" in Christian County and denounced it "in the most unmistakable terms on ail occasions." Friends inside and outside the order repeatedly warned him to be more guarded, and he said the Knobbers came to regard him as one of their "deadly enemies." For months before the Edens-Green murders, he said, he slept in the middle room of his house so that the "regulators" would have to batter down two doors to reach him.

According to Harrington, a Knobber meeting held on the night of September 3, 1886, about a mile and a half from the old smelter, took up a resolution to hang him proposed by Parson Simmons, and the resolution carried. The next night Dave Walker led a force of 142 men toward Ozark, halted at the old pond on the Sparta road a mile east of town, and sent three men in to scout the most practicable plan of attack.

Harrington met the three scouts near his residence and assumed they were hunting McCormack, a Chadwick timber agent who had been whipped a few nights earlier for reporting Knobbers cutting timber and who was hiding in Ozark. Believing a raid on the town was coming, he asked the scouts how long it would be before they made the attack. Harrington supposed that this led the scouts to think he was expecting the Knobbers and ready to meet them, and the plan to attack him was abandoned.

No arrest or prosecution for the plot against Harrington appears in the coverage. By the time of the interview, Dave Walker and other Knobbers had been tried and convicted for the separate Edens-Green murders, with Harrington serving on the prosecution.

The story came from Ozark correspondence of the St. Louis Globe-Democrat and was reprinted by the Memphis Appeal on April 30, 1888, and the Butler Weekly Times on May 2. Both copies ran under the headline "A Black Mask Romance," with a deck ending "The Intended Lynching of Col. Harrington," although the plot itself took up only a short passage near the end of a long interview about the prosecution. The Memphis copy, as printed, breaks off before that passage, while the Butler Weekly Times carried it in full.

The account was given entirely in Harrington's voice and framed the Knobbers as "outlaws" in an "irrepressible" conflict with "the social security of Christian county." No independent report of the 1886 march appears in the coverage, and the copies differ on the interview date, the Memphis text giving "the 24th instant" and the Butler dateline April 21.

accounts.label: Harrington's interview (Globe-Democrat correspondence)
accounts.gist: A Knobber meeting voted to hang Harrington; Dave Walker led 142 men toward Ozark the next night, but after Harrington questioned their scouts about when the attack would come, the Knobbers believed he was ready for them and abandoned the plan.

framing.detail: The Globe-Democrat story, headlined 'A Black Mask Romance' with 'The Intended Lynching of Col. Harrington' in the deck, presents the prosecutor's account of 'outlaws' as fact.

conflicts.note: Concerns the 1888 interview, not the 1886 plot; the Butler date may be an OCR or editing variant.
